title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Reading the Balance Sheet Behind the Eyewear Growth

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion; cash flow and return on invested capital are facts.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: A forensic audit of Lenskart's consolidated statements (FY2020–FY2026, TTM, and Sep 2026) shows a sharp operational inflection [1]. Yet the balance sheet still reflects heavy M&A, Ind AS 116 lease capitalization, and factory capex. Below are the complete audited snapshot statements:

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Profit & Loss Statement (FY2020–FY2026 & TTM, ₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue compounded ~46% annually from ₹900 Cr (FY20) to ₹8,814 Cr (FY26) and ₹10,383 Cr (TTM), while OPM expanded from -8% (FY22) to 19.9% (FY26) and 21% (TTM).

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Balance Sheet (Mar 2020–Sep 2026, ₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Total assets expanded nearly 6x from ₹2,583 Cr (Mar 2020) to ₹15,677 Cr (Sep 2026), driven by ₹8,358 Cr in Fixed Assets (including RoU lease assets and Owndays goodwill/intangibles) and ₹3,455 Cr in Borrowings (primarily lease liabilities).

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Cash Flow Statement (FY2020–FY2026, ₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow turned positive in FY23 (₹95 Cr) and scaled to ₹1,231 Cr (FY25) and ₹1,670 Cr (FY26), generating ₹805 Cr and ₹846 Cr of Free Cash Flow in FY25 and FY26 respectively.

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Return Ratios (FY2020–FY2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days compressed from 27 (FY23) to 7 (FY25–FY26) and Cash Conversion Cycle tightened to 19 days in FY26, while ROCE improved from -3% (FY22) to 8% (FY26).

web_blocks.html: Five forensic findings emerge when we cross-examine the P&L, Balance Sheet, Cash Flow, and Ratios together:

web_blocks.title: Forensic Finding 1: Ind AS 116 Lease Capitalization & Balance-Sheet Bloat
paragraphs: Fixed Assets leaped from ₹649 crore (Mar 2022) to ₹5,067 crore (Mar 2023) and ₹8,358 crore (Sep 2026) after Owndays and COCO store rollouts [1]. Borrowings jumped from ₹34 crore to ₹934 crore (Mar 2023), ₹2,740 crore (Mar 2025), and ₹3,455 crore (Sep 2026) [1].

Ind AS 116 capitalizes store leases as Right-of-Use assets and liabilities. Depreciation swelled from ₹85 crore (FY22) to ₹1,048 crore (FY26) and ₹1,183 crore (TTM), while Interest hit ₹178 crore [1]. Statutory CFO looks strong at ₹1,670 crore in FY26, but lease principal payments sit in financing cash flows; pre-Ind AS CFO is closer to ₹887 crore [1][12].

web_blocks.html: Second, capital efficiency (ROE and ROCE) remains depressed. Consolidated ROCE is 8.08% and ROE is 6.55% (3-year average ROE: 3.90%) [1]. Three factors explain this drag: a ₹9,322 crore equity base (post-IPO), ₹8,358 crore fixed assets plus ₹245 crore CWIP, and Owndays/Meller goodwill [1][6][9]. Capital turns will stay muted until the Hyderabad plant ramps and Owndays margins expand.

Third, working capital discipline improved sharply. Point-of-sale cash collection cut Debtor Days from 27 days (FY23) to 7 days (FY25–FY26) [1]. Inventory Days remain high at 150 days (down from 198 in FY25), but 138 Payable Days finance that stock. The Cash Conversion Cycle compressed from 69 days in FY25 to 19 days in FY26 [1].

Fourth, earnings quality needs monitoring. Screener flags that Lenskart 'might be capitalizing the interest cost' alongside ₹245 crore CWIP [1]. FY25 PAT (₹297 crore) also leaned on ₹351 crore of Other Income [1][11]. Encouragingly, FY26 PAT (₹501 crore) and TTM PAT (₹797 crore) were driven by core operating profit (₹1,754 crore FY26; ₹2,209 crore TTM) [1].

Fifth, investing outflows remain heavy. Investing Cash Flow was -₹2,586 crore in FY23 and -₹2,551 crore in FY26 (Meller stake, ₹824 crore capex, and IPO treasury deployments) [1][4][9]. Equity Capital expanded to ₹347 crore and Reserves reached ₹8,974 crore by September 2026 [1]. With zero dividends, shareholder returns depend entirely on high-ROIC incremental store and factory execution [1][4].

To judge Lenskart's balance sheet fairly, separate operating cash generation from capital intensity. In FY26, operating cash flow hit ₹1,670 crore—covering ₹824 crore of capex more than twice over and yielding ₹846 crore of free cash flow [1]. Even after stripping out Ind AS 116 lease principal payments, pre-Ind AS cash flow turned solidly positive [1][11]. Yet consolidated ROCE sits at 8.08% and ROE at 6.55% because equity (₹9,322 crore) and fixed assets (₹8,358 crore plus ₹245 crore CWIP) grew rapidly through IPO proceeds and M&A [1]. Lifting ROE above 15% requires higher asset turns from Hyderabad and Owndays.

book_paragraphs: If you want to separate a genuine compounder from a well-marketed story, you open the seven-year financial statements and trace every rupee from the income statement to the balance sheet and cash flow statement. For Lenskart, those statements tell a tale of two halves: explosive operational scaling on the top line, paired with a capital-heavy balance sheet that is only now beginning to earn its keep.

Look at the Profit and Loss statement first. Between FY20 and FY26, consolidated revenue grew nearly tenfold, from ₹900 crore to ₹8,814 crore—and crossed ₹10,383 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026. Operating profit swung from a ₹115 crore loss in FY22 to ₹1,754 crore in FY26 and ₹2,209 crore TTM. That is unmistakable operating leverage.

Now flip to the Balance Sheet and ask why Return on Capital Employed is still only 8.08% and Return on Equity is just 6.55%. The answer sits in two places: ₹9,322 crore of shareholder equity raised across private rounds and the 2025 IPO, and ₹8,358 crore of fixed assets—inflated by Ind AS 116 Right-of-Use store leases, Owndays and Meller acquisition goodwill, and automated plant capex.

book_subsections.title: Cash Flow Forensics, Working Capital & Watchpoints
paragraphs: There is genuine good news on working capital and cash generation. Because customers pay at the counter or online, Lenskart's debtor days dropped from 27 days in FY23 to just 7 days in FY26. Even though carrying thousands of frame styles keeps inventory at 150 days, Lenskart stretches supplier payables to 138 days, leaving a lean 19-day cash conversion cycle. As a result, statutory Free Cash Flow turned decisively positive—reaching ₹805 crore in FY25 and ₹846 crore in FY26.

Still, you and I must keep three forensic yellow flags taped to our desk. First, statutory CFO of ₹1,670 crore excludes roughly ₹780 crore of lease principal payments sitting in financing cash flows. Second, FY25's profit inflection leaned heavily on ₹351 crore of Other Income, though FY26 and TTM earnings proved core operating leverage has now taken the wheel. Third, with ₹245 crore of Capital Work-in-Progress for Hyderabad and automated forensics flagging potential interest capitalization, we must watch asset turns closely as the new plant comes online.

book_subsections.title: Balance Sheet Reality: Leases, Capex Intensity & Single-Digit ROE
paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic accountant's hat and examine why a business with 21% trailing operating margins still reports a 6.55% ROE and an 8.08% ROCE. Start with the balance sheet as of September 2026: total shareholders' equity stands at ₹9,322 Cr—bolstered by the ₹2,150 Cr fresh IPO proceeds raised in November 2025—against ₹3,455 Cr of borrowings (primarily capitalized Ind AS 116 store lease liabilities rather than bank term debt) and ₹8,358 Cr of net fixed assets plus ₹245 Cr of capital work-in-progress.

Because Lenskart operates thousands of leased retail stores and capital-intensive manufacturing plants, Ind AS 116 splits store rent into depreciation (₹1,048 Cr in FY26, ₹1,183 Cr TTM) and lease interest (₹178 Cr in FY26, ₹199 Cr TTM). That accounting treatment flatters statutory EBITDA (₹1,754 Cr in FY26) relative to true cash operating profit (~₹1,000–₹1,032 Cr pre-Ind AS) while weighing on return on capital employed until new stores and the Hyderabad plant reach peak utilization.

The good news is that earnings quality on the cash flow statement is genuine: FY26 operating cash flow of ₹1,670 Cr comfortably exceeded statutory net profit of ₹501 Cr, and even after ₹824 Cr of growth capex, free cash flow hit ₹846 Cr. Still, investors must monitor two forensic watchpoints: first, Screener's flag regarding potential interest-cost capitalization during heavy factory construction; and second, whether ROE can climb from 6.55% into the mid-teens over FY27–FY29 as IPO cash is deployed into high-returning Indian stores rather than lower-margin international M&A.

book_subsections.title: Separating Real Cash Compounding from Accounting Optics
paragraphs: If there is one financial lesson I want you to carry from Chapter 6, it is never to value a multi-thousand-store retailer on statutory Ind AS 116 EBITDA alone. Under Ind AS 116, store rent disappears from operating expenses and reappears below the EBITDA line as depreciation on right-of-use assets (₹1,048 Cr in FY26) and interest on lease liabilities (₹178 Cr in FY26). That is why Lenskart's statutory FY26 operating margin looks like a software-like 19.9%, whereas its true pre-Ind AS cash EBITDA margin is 14.3% in India and 7.0% internationally.

Even after adjusting for leases, however, Lenskart's cash conversion is healthy: FY26 CFO of ₹1,670 Cr covered ₹824 Cr of capex more than twice over. The true tension in the financials is not cash burn—that era is over—it is capital intensity. With ₹8,358 Cr of net fixed assets, ₹245 Cr of CWIP, and ₹9,322 Cr of equity on the September 2026 balance sheet, Lenskart must generate substantially higher asset turns from its Hyderabad plant and international stores to lift ROCE above its ~11.5% cost of capital.

book_subsections.title: The Path from 6.55% ROE to Double-Digit Capital Returns
paragraphs: For Lenskart to earn a higher return on equity over the medium term, two levers must fire simultaneously. First, the ₹2,150 Cr of fresh IPO cash sitting on the balance sheet must be deployed into high-payback Indian stores and the Hyderabad automated plant rather than low-yielding treasury instruments. Second, depreciation—which hit ₹1,048 Cr in FY26 and ₹1,183 Cr TTM—must grow slower than revenue as store maturity improves.
If net profit margins expand from 5.7% in FY26 toward 9%–10% by FY28 while asset turns hold steady, ROE can cross 13%–15%, validating the business's long-term compounding credentials.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: A Compounder With a Capital-Efficiency Homework Assignment
book_callouts.text: On pure business fundamentals—before we ever look at a share price or a chart—Lenskart earns a COMPOUNDER_PASS with a PASS_WITH_WATCH on KPIs. Few Indian consumer companies have built a ₹10,000+ crore revenue omnichannel platform with ~70% gross margins and positive free cash flow. Yet single-digit ROE and ROCE, Ind AS 116 lease weight, and 17.52% promoter ownership mean this is not a frictionless asset-light compounder. How much of that execution is already priced in—or still unappreciated—is the question we will answer only after we examine valuation and market structure.
